record.original_question: Let X be a nuclear F-space in the sense defined via diametral approximative dimension. Is every unconditionally convergent series in X necessarily absolutely convergent?

artifact.status_search_result: The classical Dvoretzky–Rogers theorem (and its locally convex extension by Grothendieck/Pietsch) shows that unconditional convergence implies absolute convergence in nuclear Fréchet (locally convex) spaces. For non-locally-convex nuclear F-spaces defined via diametral approximative dimension, no resolution was located in the search; the question appears to remain unresolved in the literature accessible online.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Definitions. An F-space is a complete metrizable topological vector space whose topology is given by a translation-invariant metric (not necessarily locally convex). For a bounded subset B of an F-space X and ε>0, let N(ε,B) denote the smallest cardinality of an ε-net for B (in the invariant metric), and define the diametral approximative dimension of X as the collection of all sequences (t_n) of positive reals such that for every neighborhood U of 0 there is a neighborhood V of 0 with t_n · δ_n(V,U) → 0, where δ_n(V,U) is the n-th Kolmogorov diameter of V with respect to U. Call an F-space X nuclear (in the sense of diametral approximative dimension) if its diametral approximative dimension contains every sequence (t_n) of positive reals tending to infinity, equivalently if it satisfies the Kolmogorov diameter characterization of nuclearity adapted to F-spaces.

A series ∑ x_n in X is said to converge unconditionally if ∑ x_{π(n)} converges in X for every permutation π of ℕ. It is said to converge absolutely if for every continuous F-seminorm (equivalently, for the invariant metric d) one has ∑ d(x_n, 0) < ∞.

Question. Let X be a nuclear F-space in the above sense. Is it true that every unconditionally convergent series in X is absolutely convergent?
